title: Belling the Cat
text:
The mice lived in terror of the cat. It moved so quietly that it was on top of them before they knew it, and every week another mouse disappeared. At last they called a council to decide what to do.

Many ideas were put forward and rejected. Then a young mouse stood up with a plan that seemed brilliant. The danger, he said, was that they never heard the cat coming. So they should hang a bell around its neck. Whenever the cat moved, the bell would ring, and every mouse would have time to run to its hole.

The council cheered. The plan was simple and clever, and everyone agreed it would save them all. In the middle of the applause an old mouse, who had said nothing so far, got up and asked one question: which of them was going to put the bell on the cat?

The room went silent. The mice looked at one another, and then at the floor. Nobody volunteered, and the meeting broke up with the cat still unbelled.
lesson: A plan everyone applauds is worth nothing until someone has agreed to carry out the hardest step. Ask who will do it before you celebrate the idea.
date: Medieval fable tradition, attributed to Aesop
source: Aesop's Fables, The Mice in Council; Odo of Cheriton, Fabulae
caveat: Although usually listed with Aesop, the fable is first found in medieval collections such as that of Odo of Cheriton.
